newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine stocks close higher, seen topping out.
newsitem.headline: Argentine stocks close higher, seen topping out.

text.p: Argentina's bolsa recouped midsession losses and struggled higher at the close Tuesday, but traders said it rubbed up against stiff technical resistance.

"With current slim volumes the market is oversold and 561 is a pretty tough hurdle for the (blue-chip) MerVal index," said Jorge Bonanno at Interfin brokers. "Stocks shrugged off a new drop in the U.S. long bond yield, which means they could be headed for a pullback."
The weighted MerVal added 0.4 percent to 560.99, continuing the mild-mannered advance of the past four weeks.
Traders said the market was underpinned by Argentina's 10-year global bond issue, which was expanded to $1.0 billion from $750 million Wednesday due to strong demand.
The bond, due to be priced Wednesday at between 445-450 points above the comparable U.S. Treasury note, was expected to yield around 11.2 percent which traders described as no more than decent.

"It's a reasonable rate, which is pretty much in line with what we have today in the domestic market," said broker Luis Corsiglia. "It seems for now it's pretty much the same to renew debt here or abroad."
The bolsa's broad market index inched up 0.1 percent Tuesday, with losers and gainers tied at 22 in the session and 20 stocks closing flat.
Floor volume remained weak at 13.6 million pesos compared to 11.8 million Monday, while over-the-counter turnover swelled to 84.6 million pesos from 53.8 million Monday.
Top main-tier performances were put in by steelmaker Acindar, Banco Frances and foods giant Molinos Rio de la Plata, which advanced 2.4 percent, 2.3 percent and 2.1 percent, respectively.
MerVal losers were led by construction stock Polledo, which fell 1.0 percent, carmaker Sevel, which shed 0.9 percent, and holding company Comercial del Plata, off 0.8 percent.

Second-tier stock Baesa, the Pepsi bottler, extended Monday's 15 percent nosedive with a new 5.7 percent drop on PepsiCo's decision to downsize its Brazil operations and focus on other markets, traders said.
